pages.text: Under the shade of the courtyard tree, Nana Yaw stood beside two tall wooden drums. ‘These are the atumpan,’ said Nana Yaw. ‘They are the talking drums of the Akan people.’ Kwame’s eyes grew wide. ‘Can a drum really talk, Nana?’
sentences: Under the shade of the courtyard tree, Nana Yaw stood beside two tall wooden drums.
‘These are the atumpan,’ said Nana Yaw.
‘They are the talking drums of the Akan people.’ Kwame’s eyes grew wide.
‘Can a drum really talk, Nana?’
pages.alt: Six-year-old Kwame looks up in wonder at two tall carved wooden atumpan drums beside his grandfather Nana Yaw.

pages.text: Nana Yaw held up two curved wooden sticks shaped like the letter L. ‘One drum has a low voice, kon-kon,’ he said. ‘The other drum has a high voice, ka-la. Together, their low and high tones sound like spoken words.’
sentences: Nana Yaw held up two curved wooden sticks shaped like the letter L.
‘One drum has a low voice, kon-kon,’ he said.
‘The other drum has a high voice, ka-la.
Together, their low and high tones sound like spoken words.’
pages.alt: Nana Yaw holds two curved L-shaped drumsticks above the pair of atumpan drums.

pages.text: Kwame was so excited that he took the sticks and tapped as fast as he could. Bam-bam-bam! The sound was loud and messy. Cousin Esi covered her ears and giggled. ‘Slow down, Kwame!’ she laughed.
sentences: Kwame was so excited that he took the sticks and tapped as fast as he could.
Bam-bam-bam!
The sound was loud and messy.
Cousin Esi covered her ears and giggled.
‘Slow down, Kwame!’ she laughed.
pages.alt: Kwame taps the drums too fast with a big grin while Cousin Esi covers her ears and giggles.

pages.text: Nana Yaw gently placed his hand over Kwame’s hands. ‘A good drummer is first a good listener,’ said Nana Yaw. ‘Listen with your ears. Listen with your heart. Then let your hands answer.’
sentences: Nana Yaw gently placed his hand over Kwame’s hands.
‘A good drummer is first a good listener,’ said Nana Yaw.
‘Listen with your ears.
Listen with your heart.
Then let your hands answer.’
pages.alt: Nana Yaw gently rests his warm hands over Kwame’s hands on the drumsticks.

pages.text: ‘Does everyone in Ghana play the same drum?’ asked Esi. ‘No,’ smiled Nana Yaw. ‘Ghana has many wonderful traditions. Here in Ashanti we play the atumpan. In northern Ghana, drummers tuck the lunna hourglass drum under one arm and squeeze its cords to talk. And in your home in the Volta Region, Esi, Ewe master drummers play the tall atsimevu with a stick and bare hand.’
sentences: ‘Does everyone in Ghana play the same drum?’ asked Esi.
‘No,’ smiled Nana Yaw.
‘Ghana has many wonderful traditions.
Here in Ashanti we play the atumpan.
In northern Ghana, drummers tuck the lunna hourglass drum under one arm and squeeze its cords to talk.
And in your home in the Volta Region, Esi, Ewe master drummers play the tall atsimevu with a stick and bare hand.’
pages.alt: Nana Yaw shows Kwame and Esi a carved wooden lunna hourglass drum and a tall Ewe drum on the veranda.

pages.text: Now Kwame stood still and closed his eyes to listen. Nana Yaw tapped a slow welcome greeting on the two drums: ‘Kon-kon, ka-la! Kon-kon, ka-la! Akwaaba, welcome all!’
sentences: Now Kwame stood still and closed his eyes to listen.
Nana Yaw tapped a slow welcome greeting on the two drums: ‘Kon-kon, ka-la!
Kon-kon, ka-la!
Akwaaba, welcome all!’
pages.alt: Kwame closes his eyes and listens carefully while Nana Yaw taps the two atumpan drums.

pages.text: Kwame opened his eyes and breathed in slowly. He lifted the curved sticks and echoed the rhythm carefully: ‘Kon-kon, ka-la! Kon-kon, ka-la!’ This time the low drum and the high drum spoke clearly together.
sentences: Kwame opened his eyes and breathed in slowly.
He lifted the curved sticks and echoed the rhythm carefully: ‘Kon-kon, ka-la!
Kon-kon, ka-la!’ This time the low drum and the high drum spoke clearly together.
pages.alt: Kwame plays the two atumpan drums carefully with the curved sticks while Nana Yaw nods proudly.

pages.text: Neighbors gathered in the courtyard and smiled as they heard the welcome call. Esi clapped in time with the beat, and Nana Yaw beamed. Kwame had learned the secret of the talking drum: when you listen first, your music speaks to everyone. The end.
sentences: Neighbors gathered in the courtyard and smiled as they heard the welcome call.
Esi clapped in time with the beat, and Nana Yaw beamed.
Kwame had learned the secret of the talking drum: when you listen first, your music speaks to everyone.
The end.
pages.alt: Neighbours gather smiling in the sunny courtyard as Kwame and Nana Yaw play the welcome rhythm together.

activities.question: How do the two atumpan drums imitate spoken words?
options: One drum plays a low tone and the other plays a high tone
A small radio is hidden inside the wood
They only make one loud sound
activities.explanation: Akan is a tonal language, so the low-toned and high-toned drums mimic the tones of spoken phrases.

activities.question: What did Nana Yaw say a good drummer must be first?
options: The loudest person in the yard
activities.explanation: Nana Yaw taught Kwame that a good drummer is first a good listener.

activities.question: Do all communities across Ghana play the exact same drums?
options: No; each region has its own drums, like atumpan, lunna and atsimevu
Yes; every town in Ghana only has one kind of drum
No; drums are only played in schools
activities.explanation: Ghana’s cultural traditions are diverse, with distinct instruments and styles across Akan, Dagomba, Ewe and other communities.

activities.prompt: Which word starts with the dr sound, like drum?

items: Nana Yaw shows Kwame the two atumpan drums and curved sticks.
Kwame beats the drums too fast without listening.
Nana Yaw teaches Kwame to stop and listen to the rhythm first.
Kwame echoes the welcome rhythm clearly for the neighbours.

activities.prompt: When someone is speaking or teaching you something new, how does listening carefully help?

glossary.definition: An open space surrounded by walls or rooms inside a family home.
High or low musical and spoken sounds.
Someone who pays close attention to what they hear.
Customs, music and ways of life passed down from older generations.
A regular, repeated pattern of beats or sounds.
